claim: The locus coeruleus (LC) is the major source of norepinephrine (NE) to the brain.
source: The major source of NE to the brain is the locus coeruleus (LC), a small structure in the brainstem.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction and is established scientific knowledge about the LC's role in the brain.

claim: The NE-LC system has widespread efferents to almost the entire brain.
source: The NE-LC system has widespread efferents to almost the entire brain and can modulate cognition, behavior and autonomic tone via its effects on adrenoreceptors in target neurons (Sara, 2009; Sara and Bouret, 2012; Samuels and Szabadi, 2008a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Sara, 2009; Sara and Bouret, 2012; Samuels and Szabadi, 2008a).

claim: The NE-LC system can modulate cognition, behavior and autonomic tone via its effects on adrenoreceptors in target neurons.
source: The NE-LC system has widespread efferents to almost the entire brain and can modulate cognition, behavior and autonomic tone via its effects on adrenoreceptors in target neurons (Sara, 2009; Sara and Bouret, 2012; Samuels and Szabadi, 2008a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Sara, 2009; Sara and Bouret, 2012; Samuels and Szabadi, 2008a).

claim: Blocking β-adrenergic receptors in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) immediately after learning in arousing conditions impairs memory in rodents.
source: Rodent work consistently demonstrated that blocking β-adrenergic receptors in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) immediately after learning in arousing conditions impairs memory, while infusion of NE or β-adrenoreceptor agonists enhances consolidation and rescinds the impairment, evaluated one to two days later (Roozendaal et al., 2008; Power et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to rodent studies (Roozendaal et al., 2008; Power et al., 2002).

claim: Infusion of NE or β-adrenoreceptor agonists in the BLA enhances consolidation and rescinds memory impairment in rodents.
source: Rodent work consistently demonstrated that blocking β-adrenergic receptors in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) immediately after learning in arousing conditions impairs memory, while infusion of NE or β-adrenoreceptor agonists enhances consolidation and rescinds the impairment, evaluated one to two days later (Roozendaal et al., 2008; Power et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to rodent studies (Roozendaal et al., 2008; Power et al., 2002).

claim: Stimulation of the LC during the learning phase modulates activity in the BLA and synaptic plasticity in the CA1, CA3 and dentate gyrus.
source: Correspondingly, stimulation of the LC during the learning phase modulates activity in the BLA and synaptic plasticity in the CA1, CA3 and dentate gyrus (Lemon et al., 2009; Wagatsuma et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Lemon et al., 2009; Wagatsuma et al., 2018).

claim: Blocking β-adrenoreceptors prior to learning had no effect on subsequent retrieval 24 hr later in rodents.
source: While these studies highlight the importance of adrenergic signaling for plasticity and hippocampal-dependent learning, blocking β-adrenoreceptors prior to learning had no effect on subsequent retrieval 24 hr later (Wagatsuma et al., 2018; Khakpour-Taleghani et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Wagatsuma et al., 2018; Khakpour-Taleghani et al., 2008).

claim: Administration of propranolol 90 min before encoding attenuated expected amygdala responses during encoding of emotional stimuli in humans.
source: In humans, administration of propranolol 90 min before encoding attenuated expected amygdala responses during encoding of emotional stimuli, and even though the propranolol was eliminated at retrieval, hippocampal responses during retrieval of emotional stimuli were absent (Strange and Dolan, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a human study (Strange and Dolan, 2004).

claim: Hippocampal responses during retrieval of emotional stimuli were absent when propranolol was administered before encoding, even though the propranolol was eliminated at retrieval.
source: In humans, administration of propranolol 90 min before encoding attenuated expected amygdala responses during encoding of emotional stimuli, and even though the propranolol was eliminated at retrieval, hippocampal responses during retrieval of emotional stimuli were absent (Strange and Dolan, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a human study (Strange and Dolan, 2004).

claim: Propranolol impaired memory accuracy for emotional events and decreased saliva measures of NE in humans.
source: In addition, propranolol impaired memory accuracy for emotional events and decreased saliva measures of NE (Hermans et al., 2014; McIntyre et al., 2003; Strange and Dolan, 2004; Cahill et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human studies (Hermans et al., 2014; McIntyre et al., 2003; Strange and Dolan, 2004; Cahill et al., 1994).

claim: Increases in NE-tone during encoding, but not during retrieval, modulated memory performance in humans.
source: In humans, increases in NE-tone during encoding, but not during retrieval, modulated memory performance (Rimmele et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a human study (Rimmele et al., 2016).

claim: Twenty-seven young right-handed adults (13 female, 20–30 years, mean ± SD = 22.95±1.96) underwent 7T MR imaging in this study.
source: Twenty-seven young right-handed adults (13 female, 20–30 years, mean ± SD = 22.95±1.96) underwent 7T MR imaging which included structural scans (T1-weighted scan, dedicated LC imaging) and ultra-high-resolution blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signal fMRI.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study participants and methods.

claim: All participants performed the task above chance level in recollection (33.3%), with a median number of hits of 48.33% (IQR = 40.78, 54.89).
source: All participants performed the task above chance level in recollection (33.3%), with a median number of hits (correctly recollected) of 48.33% (IQR = 40.78, 54.89) and median number of miss rate (incorrectly recollected) of 51.67% (IQR = 45.11, 59.22).
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data from the study.

claim: There was no significant difference between the recognition hit rate for emotional compared to neutral faces.
source: There was no significant difference (Wilcoxon paired test: Z = −1.17, p-value=0.244) between the recognition hit rate for emotional (Median = 53.33% (IQR = 45.56, 61.11)) compared to neutral faces (Median = 53.33% (IQR = 44.44, 67.79, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: More false alarms were detected for emotional compared to neutral faces during recognition.
source: However, more false alarms were detected (Wilcoxon paired test: Z = 3.81, p-value<o0.001) for emotional (Median = 22.73% (IQR = 18.19, 34.09) compared to neutral faces (Median = 13.63% (IQR = 9.09, 22.78); Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: There was a bias in misclassifying emotional faces during recognition.
source: A paired t-test revealed a bias in misclassifying emotional faces during recognition (t(27)=5.34, p-value<0.001, Figure 2B) and a higher response bias for the emotional recognition condition (t(27)=2.49, p-value=0.019, Figure 2C), towards responding that they had seen the face before.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and reference to Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Participants recollected on average more names with an emotional relative to those with a neutral valence after correcting for bias.
source: Repeating the analysis after correcting for the bias (partial residuals), showed that participants recollected on average more names with an emotional (median = 38.68, IQR = 36.68, 39.46) relative to those with a neutral valence (median = 29.97, IQR = 28.01, 33.39; paired Wilcoxon test: Z = 4.41, p-value<0.001, Figure 2G), in accordance with an expected memory advantage for emotional trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of bias-corrected behavioral data and reference to Figure 2G.

claim: A significant increase in sAA was observed during consolidation relative to encoding.
source: Linear mixed effects models with ΔsAA across the task stages revealed an increase in ΔsAA during consolidation relative to encoding (β = −65.95, t(47.92) = −2.91, p=0.033, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of sAA data and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: There was a positive, at trend level, association between ΔsAA during consolidation and emotional memory performance.
source: To further probe the increase in ΔsAA during consolidation, correlation analyses showed a positive, at trend level, association with emotional memory performance (r = 0.452, N = 18, p-value=0.059, Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and reference to Figure 3B.

claim: A negative relationship was observed between ΔsAA and rMSSD across the task stages.
source: Given that both measures relate to the autonomic system, we then correlated ΔsAA to RMSSD across the stages using bootstrapped (n = 5000) repeated measures correlations and observed a negative relationship (Rrm(df)=−0.387,(35), p=0.018, CI (95%)=[−0.638,–0.061], Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by repeated measures correlation analysis and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: A bilateral LC component was identified using brainstem-specific group-level independent-component-analyses (ICA) on the baseline resting-state fMRI.
source: Using brainstem-specific group-level independent-component-analyses (ICA) on the baseline resting-state fMRI in combination with a custom anatomical LC template from our MT-TFL sequence, we identified a bilateral LC component (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ICA analysis method and reference to Figure 4A and B.

claim: A negative correlation was observed between LC variance and rMSSD across task stages.
source: Consistent with our previous analyses, we applied repeated measures correlation and observed a negative correlation between LC variance and rMSSD across task stages (Rrm(df)=−0.326,(63), p-value=0.008, CI (95%)=[−0.531,–0.084], Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by repeated measures correlation analysis and reference to Figure 4C.

claim: No correlation was found between rMSSD and variance in a control region (a component close to the 4th ventricle).
source: We found no correlation between rMSSD and variance in a control region, a component close to the 4th ventricle that explained a similar amount of variance in the ICA (Rrm(df)=−0.201(63), p=0.11, CI (95%)=[−0.494, 0.427], Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by repeated measures correlation analysis and reference to Figure 4D.

claim: No correlation was observed between LC variance and ΔsAA.
source: We also observed no correlation between LC variance and ΔsAA (Rrm(df)=−0.006,(38), p-value=0.971, CI (95%)=[−0.325, 0.314], Figure 4E) or between the reference component variance and ΔsAA (Rrm(df)=−0.012,(38), p-value=0.943, CI (95%)=[−0.309, 0.330], Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by repeated measures correlation analysis and reference to Figure 4E.

claim: Greater LC-HRV coherence levels were observed during baseline compared to consolidation.
source: Greater LC-HRV coherence levels were observed during baseline compared to consolidation (β = −0.20, t(7889) = −6.65, p<0.001, RoS:<0.27 Hz), during encoding compared to consolidation (β = 0.13, t(7889) = 4.31, p<0.001, RoS:<0.29 Hz), during recollection compared to baseline (β = −0.20, t(7889) = −6.55, p<0.001, RoS:>0.25 Hz) and during recollection compared to encoding (β = −0.12, t(7889) = −4.17, p<0.001, RoS:>0.27 Hz; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed effects model analysis and reference to Figure 5C.

claim: A negative relationship was observed between LC-HRV median coherence and ΔsAA.
source: We observed a negative relationship between LC-HRV median coherence and ΔsAA (Rrm(df)=−0.383 (34), p-value=0.021, CI (95%)=[−0.64,–0.05], Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by repeated measures correlation analysis and reference to Figure 5E.

claim: No significant relationship was observed between reference component-HRV coherence and ΔsAA.
source: Additionally, we repeated this analysis for the reference component, but observed no significant relationship with ΔsAA (Rrm(df)=0.218 (34), p-value=0.201, CI (95%)=[−0.13, 0.52], Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by repeated measures correlation analysis and reference to Figure 5F.

claim: The GLM revealed activation in the CA1 and 3, bilateral BLA (extending into the centromedial amygdala) and right entorhinal cortex during successful encoding versus no successful encoding.
source: The GLM within our predefined mask (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) largely confirmed this, by showing activation in the CA1 and 3, bilateral BLA (extending into the centromedial amygdala) and right entorhinal cortex during successful encoding versus no successful encoding (Supplementary file 8A, Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLM analysis results and reference to Figure 6A and Supplementary file 8A.

claim: Significant bilateral LC activation was observed for high arousal events (High Arousal > Low Arousal) during encoding.
source: The high arousal (local HRV minima) events (High Arousal > Low Arousal) showed significant bilateral activation at the LC (peak z-value = 3.3, Figure 6C), consistent with our previous results examining HRV-LC coherence during encoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by GLM analysis results and reference to Figure 6C.

claim: Significant voxels of LC activation were observed for the interaction of high compared to low arousal during successful encoding.
source: In addition, significant voxels of LC activation were observed for the interaction of high compared to low arousal during successful encoding (High Arousal successful Encoding > Low Arousal successful Encoding; peak z-value = 5.2; Figure 6B), successfully encoding versus forgotten trials during high arousal (High Arousal successful Encoding > High Arousal forgotten, peak z-value = 2.9, Figure 6D) and bilaterally for encoding of emotional stimuli relative to neutral during high arousal (High Arousal Emotional Encoding > High Arousal Neutral Encoding, peak z-value = 5.8, Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLM analysis results and reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Higher LC activity in emotionally encoded trials under high arousal as compared to neutral trials was related to better memory performance.
source: The extracted beta-coefficients of this contrast correlated with emotional memory performance (r = 0.506, N = 24, p=0.019), indicating that higher LC activity in emotionally encoded trials under high arousal as compared to neutral trials was related to better memory performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between LC beta-coefficients and memory performance.

claim: The GLM revealed activation in the left CA1 and subiculum for successful recollection.
source: The GLM revealed activation in the left CA1 and subiculum for successful recollection (Supplementary file 8B, Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLM analysis results and reference to Figure 6F and Supplementary file 8B.

claim: A decrease in functional connectivity was observed during consolidation compared to baseline between the LC and left BLA, (para)subiculum and EC.
source: We observed a decrease in FC during consolidation compared to baseline between the LC and left BLA, (para)subiculum and EC (Supplementary file 8C, Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analysis and reference to Figure 7A and Supplementary file 8C.

claim: An increase in HIP-AMY coherence was observed for encoding compared to baseline.
source: We observed an increase in HIP-AMY coherence for encoding compared to baseline (β = −0.13, t(821)=-4.39, p<0.001, 95% CI[−0.20,–0.052]), a decrease in recollection compared to encoding (β = 0.10, t(821)=3.37, p=0.004, 95% CI[0.023, 0.171]) and a trend for consolidation decrease compared to baseline (β = −0.07, t(821)=-2.35, p=0.088 95% CI[−0.141, 0.007]) and a change in phase from AMY leading the LC in encoding to the LC leading the AMY in recollection (β = 0.91, t(821)=2.73, p=0.033, 95% CI[0.051,1.772] Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear mixed effects model analysis and reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Greater memory performance was associated with greater AMY-EC coherence during encoding.
source: When relating emotional memory to coherence for these ROI pairs using linear regressions (adjusted for baseline coherence), we observed that greater memory performance was associated with greater AMY-EC coherence during encoding (β = 0.28, t(21)=2.62, p=0.038, 95% CI[0.057,0.508]), and EC-HIP coherence during encoding (at trend level: β = 0.27, t(21)=2.38, p=0.054, 95% CI[0.033,0.512]).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis relating coherence to memory performance.

claim: The LC TFL intensity normalized to a pontine tegmentum ROI showed a positive correlation with emotional recollection scores.
source: The LC TFL intensity normalized to a pontine tegmentum ROI showed a positive correlation with emotional recollection scores (r = 0.56, p=0.004, Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and reference to Figure 8D.

claim: A positive correlation with emotional recollection was observed for the medial and caudal parts of the LC, but not rostral.
source: When subdividing the LC into three equisized parts (Figure 8C), we observed a positive correlation with emotional recollection (Figure 8D) for the medial (r = 0.52, p=0.009) and caudal (r = 0.43, p=0.034) parts of the LC, not rostral (r = 0.37, p=0.074).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and reference to Figure 8C and 8D.

claim: A positive relation was observed between mean TFL intensity ratio and ΔsAA during consolidation.
source: We then related the mean TFL intensity ratio to our measure of autonomic tone and observed a positive relation with ΔsAA during consolidation (r = 602, p=0.008, N = 18).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between LC structure and autonomic measures.

claim: The positive relationship between TFL intensity and ΔsAA during consolidation was only observed for the caudal part of the LC.
source: When examining the different sections of the LC, this positive relationship was only observed for the caudal part of the LC (r = 0.79, p<0.001, N = 18).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between LC subregion structure and autonomic measures.

claim: Arousal-related LC activation followed amygdala engagement during encoding.
source: Arousal-related LC activation followed amygdala engagement during encoding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the study findings.

claim: During consolidation and recollection, activation transitioned to hippocampal involvement, reflecting learning and model updating.
source: During consolidation and recollection, activation transitioned to hippocampal involvement, reflecting learning and model updating.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the study findings.

claim: NE-LC activation is dynamic and plays an arousal-controlling role.
source: NE-LC activation is dynamic, plays an arousal-controlling role, and is not sufficient but requires interactions with the amygdala to form adaptive memories of emotional experiences.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study findings.

claim: NE-LC activation is not sufficient but requires interactions with the amygdala to form adaptive memories of emotional experiences.
source: NE-LC activation is dynamic, plays an arousal-controlling role, and is not sufficient but requires interactions with the amygdala to form adaptive memories of emotional experiences.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study findings.

claim: Forming adaptive memories in response to arousing events was predominantly associated with NE-activity.
source: Consistent with previous work, we observed that forming adaptive memories in response to arousing events was predominantly associated with NE- activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings, consistent with previous work.

claim: During encoding, stimuli eliciting arousal-related autonomic changes were associated with LC activity following amygdala activation during successful learning.
source: During encoding, stimuli eliciting arousal-related autonomic changes were associated with LC activity following amygdala activation during successful learning.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: During consolidation, the role of the LC gradually changed from being arousal-driven to maintenance or updating internal models during recollection, involving predominantly hippocampal activity.
source: During consolidation, the role of the LC gradually changed from being arousal-driven to maintenance or updating internal models during recollection, involving predominantly hippocampal activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: Across the entire memory task greater variability in LC BOLD signal was associated with lower parasympathetic activity (rMSSD).
source: Activation of the LC occurs in parallel with the autonomic system, and modulates cognition: across the entire memory task greater variability in LC BOLD signal was associated with lower parasympathetic activity (rMSSD), which in turn was associated with greater sympathetic modulation (ΔsAA) and better memory performance.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: Lower parasympathetic activity (rMSSD) was associated with greater sympathetic modulation (ΔsAA) and better memory performance.
source: Activation of the LC occurs in parallel with the autonomic system, and modulates cognition: across the entire memory task greater variability in LC BOLD signal was associated with lower parasympathetic activity (rMSSD), which in turn was associated with greater sympathetic modulation (ΔsAA) and better memory performance.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: Structural properties of the LC, the middle section, related to better emotional memory performance.
source: Beyond function, we also observed that structural properties of the LC, the middle section, related to better emotional memory performance, and greater caudal LC intensity was related to greater NE.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: Greater caudal LC intensity was related to greater NE.
source: Beyond function, we also observed that structural properties of the LC, the middle section, related to better emotional memory performance, and greater caudal LC intensity was related to greater NE.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: The rostral and middle part of the LC project densely to higher-order associative regions of the brain.
source: These correlations fit with the well-described topographic projections of the LC, where the rostral and middle part project densely to higher-order associative regions of the brain and the caudal part of the LC to the nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (Sara, 2009; Samuels and Szabadi, 2008a), which both modulate the parasympathetic outflow based on sympathetic signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Sara, 2009; Samuels and Szabadi, 2008a).

claim: The caudal part of the LC projects to the nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, which both modulate the parasympathetic outflow based on sympathetic signals.
source: These correlations fit with the well-described topographic projections of the LC, where the rostral and middle part project densely to higher-order associative regions of the brain and the caudal part of the LC to the nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (Sara, 2009; Samuels and Szabadi, 2008a), which both modulate the parasympathetic outflow based on sympathetic signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Sara, 2009; Samuels and Szabadi, 2008a).

claim: During consolidation, increases in sAA correlated positively with emotional performance.
source: During consolidation, we observed a different LC-MTL functional connectivity coupling relative to baseline, possibly reflecting transient processes related to less parasympathetic tone (lower coherence in the high frequency domain). Correspondingly, increases in sAA during consolidation correlated positively with emotional performance.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: Increases in sympathetic tone during consolidation may reflect arousal-related NE-synaptic consolidation processes.
source: Such increases in sympathetic tone may reflect arousal-related NE-synaptic consolidation processes (Packard et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citation to previous research (Packard et al., 1994).

claim: Synaptic consolidation represents the initial phase after learning where mnemonic representations change and new memory tracers are formed.
source: While systems consolidation requires years, synaptic consolidation represents the initial phase after learning where mnemonic representations change and new memory tracers are formed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about memory consolidation.

claim: Synaptic consolidation may be captured by the resting-state signal after learning a task.
source: Previous reports demonstrated that synaptic consolidation may be captured by the resting-state signal after learning a task (Vilberg and Davachi, 2013; Tambini et al., 2010; Jacobs et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Vilberg and Davachi, 2013; Tambini et al., 2010; Jacobs et al., 2014).

claim: During encoding, the LC was activated during (successful) acquisition of information that was associated with elevated arousal.
source: In support of this premise, we observed mainly arousal-related LC activity during encoding. During encoding, the LC was activated during (successful) acquisition of information that was associated with elevated arousal.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: Amygdala and hippocampal activation was only detected for successful learning, independent of valence of arousal.
source: However, amygdala and hippocampal activation was only detected for successful learning, independent of valence of arousal.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: Arousal-related LC-activation with neural input from amygdala-entorhinal co-activation was associated with memory enhancement.
source: Nonetheless, arousal-related LC-activation with neural input from amygdala-entorhinal co-activation was associated with memory enhancement.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: During recollection, no arousal-related activity was observed, but successful recollection was associated with CA1 activity.
source: During recollection, we observed no arousal-related activity, but successful recollection was associated with CA1 activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: Activation of β-adrenoreceptors in the CA1 during consolidation is required for later retention of the memory task, but not for the aversive component of the task.
source: Activation of β-adrenoreceptors in the CA1 during consolidation is required for later retention of the memory task, but not for the aversive component of the task (Mello-Carpes and Izquierdo, 2013; Chen et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Mello-Carpes and Izquierdo, 2013; Chen et al., 1992).

claim: During encoding, the LC is on the receiving end, in particular from the amygdala, whereas this changes to a leading role in recollection.
source: In addition to different activation patterns across stages, we also observed a switch in the role of LC's connectivity with MTL regions. During encoding, the LC is on the receiving end, in particular from the amygdala, whereas this changes to a leading role in recollection.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: The LC receives afferents from the central amygdala mainly at the periLC-region.
source: This phase switch between the LC and amygdala conforms with functional and anatomical descriptions of projections between the LC and central amygdala or BLA. The LC receives afferents from the central amygdala mainly at the periLC-region (Bergado et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Bergado et al., 2007).

claim: The central amygdala controls stress responses and is involved in salience processing and attention processes, important for efficient encoding.
source: The central amygdala controls stress responses and is involved in salience processing and attention processes, important for efficient encoding (Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; Roozendaal et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; Roozendaal et al., 1996).

claim: The BLA has memory-enhancing effects on the subiculum and CA1 via β-adrenergic mechanisms.
source: While the central amygdala has no effect on hippocampal LTP, the BLA has memory-enhancing effects on the subiculum and CA1 via β-adrenergic mechanisms (Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; Roozendaal et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; Roozendaal et al., 1996).

claim: The NE-input to the BLA arrives mainly from the LC.
source: The NE-input to the BLA arrives mainly from the LC (Chen and Sara, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Chen and Sara, 2007).

claim: The BLA does not project directly to the LC, but via a small direct projection to the central amygdala.
source: The BLA does not project directly to the LC, but via a small direct projection to the central amygdala (Bouret et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Bouret et al., 2003).

claim: NE responses from the LC can be considered as a prediction error during learning originating from information from the amygdala.
source: Recent general theories of brain function, such as the active inference theory (Friston et al., 2015), posit that NE responses from the LC can be considered as a prediction error during learning originating from information from the amygdala, whereas signals from the LC to the amygdala and cortex guide transfer of information and model updating (Sales et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks (Friston et al., 2015; Sales et al., 2019).

claim: Signals from the LC to the amygdala and cortex guide transfer of information and model updating.
source: Recent general theories of brain function, such as the active inference theory (Friston et al., 2015), posit that NE responses from the LC can be considered as a prediction error during learning originating from information from the amygdala, whereas signals from the LC to the amygdala and cortex guide transfer of information and model updating (Sales et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks (Friston et al., 2015; Sales et al., 2019).

claim: The amygdala is critical to maintain allostasis.
source: In these models, the amygdala is critical to maintain allostasis.
evidence: This is stated as part of the active inference theory framework.

claim: The central amygdala network would control the arousing physiological responses through its descending predicting signals to the brainstem.
source: The central amygdala network would control the arousing physiological responses through its descending predicting signals to the brainstem, whereas the BLA would be part of a neutral signal uncertainty network as it receives prediction errors from the LC.
evidence: This is stated as part of the active inference theory framework.

claim: The BLA would be part of a neutral signal uncertainty network as it receives prediction errors from the LC.
source: The central amygdala network would control the arousing physiological responses through its descending predicting signals to the brainstem, whereas the BLA would be part of a neutral signal uncertainty network as it receives prediction errors from the LC.
evidence: This is stated as part of the active inference theory framework.

claim: NE increases accuracy of episodic memories.
source: It has been suggested that NE increases accuracy of episodic memories (Barsegyan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Barsegyan et al., 2014).

claim: Interactions between the NE-LC, amygdala and hippocampus drive arousal-related memory processing, but transitions in interactions occur along the memory processing stages.
source: To conclude, interactions between the NE-LC, amygdala and hippocampus, drive arousal-related memory processing, but transitions in interactions occur along the memory processing stages.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: During successful encoding, high-arousal-related LC activation was observed, possibly reflecting attentional processes, in conjunction with amygdala activation.
source: During successful encoding, we observed high-arousal-related LC activation, possibly reflecting attentional processes, in conjunction with amygdala activation.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: During consolidation, LC-MTL connectivity is dynamic and associated with NE increases possibly reflecting LTP.
source: During consolidation, LC-MTL connectivity is dynamic and associated with NE increases possibly reflecting LTP.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: Consolidation gradually transitions to learning and updating internal models during recollection, which mainly involves hippocampal activity.
source: This gradually transitions to learning and updating internal models during recollection, which mainly involves hippocampal activity.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusion as a summary of the study findings.

claim: Salivary alpha-amylase (sAA) is a sensitive marker for the sympathetic nervous system, in particular NE.
source: In addition, we measured sAA, a sensitive marker for the sympathetic nervous system, in particular NE.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about sAA as a biomarker.

claim: Salivary alpha-amylase (sAA) correlates with plasma norepinephrine and shows similar dynamics.
source: Salivary alpha-amylase (sAA) is a sensitive marker for sympathetic nervous system reactivity that correlates with plasma norepinephrine and shows similar dynamics (Rohleder and Nater, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Rohleder and Nater, 2009).

claim: Root-mean square differences of successive peak-to-peak intervals (rMSSD) correlate tightly to parasympathetic activity.
source: Root-mean square differences of successive peak-to-peak intervals (rMSSD) were calculated over each time period. RMSSD correlates tightly to parasympathetic activity (Kleiger et al., 2005) and is relatively free of respiratory influences.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Kleiger et al., 2005).

claim: rMSSD is relatively free of respiratory influences.
source: Root-mean square differences of successive peak-to-peak intervals (rMSSD) were calculated over each time period. RMSSD correlates tightly to parasympathetic activity (Kleiger et al., 2005) and is relatively free of respiratory influences.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the rMSSD measure.

claim: The encoding phase consisted of the presentation of 90 face-name pairs (45 emotional- 45 neutral valence).
source: Encoding consisted of the presentation of 90 face-name pairs (45 emotional- 45 neutral valence; permission of use obtained from PERT96 group).
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1B.

claim: The recollection phase consisted of 135 trials (45 new faces, 23 with emotional valence).
source: Recollection consisted of 135 trials (45 new faces (23 with emotional valence)) for which participants had to decide if the face was presented before.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1B.

claim: Blocking β-adrenergic receptors increases HRV.
source: These results echo previous work demonstrating that blocking β-adrenoreceptor increases HRV (Bittiner and Smith, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Bittiner and Smith, 1986).

claim: Autonomic fluctuations due to emotionally salient stimuli can alter the power of frequencies in the HRV.
source: Autonomic fluctuations due to emotionally salient stimuli can alter the power of frequencies in the HRV and this can occur in concert with changes in LC BOLD responses (Bittiner and Smith, 1986; Akselrod et al., 1981; Lane et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Bittiner and Smith, 1986; Akselrod et al., 1981; Lane et al., 2009).

claim: Autonomic fluctuations due to emotionally salient stimuli can occur in concert with changes in LC BOLD responses.
source: Autonomic fluctuations due to emotionally salient stimuli can alter the power of frequencies in the HRV and this can occur in concert with changes in LC BOLD responses (Bittiner and Smith, 1986; Akselrod et al., 1981; Lane et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Bittiner and Smith, 1986; Akselrod et al., 1981; Lane et al., 2009).

claim: Greater LC activity coupled to greater parasympathetic inhibition during baseline and recollection has been associated with better discrimination between emotional versus neutral faces, attentional resources and better retrieval of context information from stored representation to perform memory task successfully.
source: These patterns indicate greater LC activity coupled to greater parasympathetic inhibition during baseline and recollection, which has been associated with better discrimination between emotional versus neutral faces, attentional resources and better retrieval of context information from stored representation to perform memory task successfully (Lane et al., 2009; Thayer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Lane et al., 2009; Thayer et al., 2012).

claim: Lower HF-HRV is associated with higher arousal.
source: On the other hand, consolidation demonstrated lower coherence compared to encoding or baseline, which is consistent with the premise that lower HF-HRV is associated with higher arousal.
evidence: This is stated as an established premise about HRV and arousal.

claim: Recollection is more likely to elicit hippocampal activity than recognition.
source: We decided to focus on recollection because of this response bias, our focus on the medial temporal lobe regions and the notion that recollection is more likely to elicit hippocampal activity than recognition (Rugg and Vilberg, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Rugg and Vilberg, 2013).

claim: The LC is a small structure in the brainstem.
source: The major source of NE to the brain is the locus coeruleus (LC), a small structure in the brainstem.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge about the LC.

claim: The amygdala is an important target region of the LC and a critical nexus in memory for arousing experiences.
source: Research into NE-modulation of emotional memory enhancement has focused largely on the amygdala (Hermans et al., 2014; Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; McIntyre et al., 2003), an important target region of the LC and a critical nexus in memory for arousing experiences.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Hermans et al., 2014; Phelps and LeDoux, 2005; McIntyre et al., 2003).

claim: The LC is involved in consolidation, but within a critical time period after learning.
source: For example, the LC is involved in consolidation, but within a critical time period after learning, the time required for the hippocampus to facilitate the reorganization and stabilization of storing information in the neocortex (Khakpour-Taleghani et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Khakpour-Taleghani et al., 2008).

claim: Release of NE due to LC-activation modulates, gates and tunes neural activity in a way that optimizes the signal-to-noise ratio.
source: This dynamic behavior stems from the idea that release of NE due to LC-activation modulates, gates and tunes neural activity in a way that optimizes the signal-to-noise ratio (Sara, 2009; Sara and Bouret, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Sara, 2009; Sara and Bouret, 2012).

claim: NE selectively reinforces brain activity and memory representations only if arousal-related LC activation occurs at the right time and magnitude.
source: Thus, NE selectively reinforces brain activity and memory representations only if arousal-related LC activation occurs at the right time and magnitude (Mather et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Mather et al., 2016).

claim: When increases in NE are coupled to arousal, they can lead to hippocampal synaptic plasticity.
source: When increases in NE are coupled to arousal, they can lead to hippocampal synaptic plasticity (Lemon et al., 2009; Hansen and Manahan-Vaughan, 2015), and facilitate the dynamic reorganization of neural networks (Bouret and Sara, 2005; Zerbi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Lemon et al., 2009; Hansen and Manahan-Vaughan, 2015).

claim: Increases in NE coupled to arousal can facilitate the dynamic reorganization of neural networks.
source: When increases in NE are coupled to arousal, they can lead to hippocampal synaptic plasticity (Lemon et al., 2009; Hansen and Manahan-Vaughan, 2015), and facilitate the dynamic reorganization of neural networks (Bouret and Sara, 2005; Zerbi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Bouret and Sara, 2005; Zerbi et al., 2019).

claim: Arousal-induced dynamic changes in LC activity and connectivity with its key target regions during task performance has not yet been examined in animals.
source: So far, arousal-induced dynamic changes in LC activity and connectivity with its key target regions during task performance has not yet been examined in animals (Zerbi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Zerbi et al., 2019).

claim: The left LC was 12 mm in length (108 voxels, 9.918 mm3) while the right LC measured 10 mm in length (103 voxels, 9.459 mm3) in the study template.
source: The left LC was 12 mm in length (108 voxels, 9.918 mm3) while the right LC measured 10 mm in length (103 voxels, 9.459 mm3).
evidence: This is a direct report of anatomical measurements from the study.

claim: Three fMRI-datasets were excluded due to technical reasons.
source: Three fMRI-datasets were excluded due to technical reasons, one due to spiking because of coil failure one due to a reconstruction error and one due to temporary failure of the response-recording device.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data exclusion in the study.
